verdict.rationale: The Hebrew adjective 'holy' (qadosh, H6918) is predicated of YHWH (the personal divine name of God) in dense clusters across the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings (108 tokens in 94 verses, with a heavy concentration in Isaiah using the formula 'Holy One of Israel'), and the Greek adjective 'holy' (hagios, G0040, 456 tokens in 241 verses) carries the same predication into the New Testament. The threefold 'holy, holy, holy' (Trisagion) in Isaiah 6:3 repeats 'holy' (qadosh) three times, which is the strongest superlative device biblical Hebrew has, paired with 'YHWH of hosts' and the earth filled with his 'glory' (kavod). Leviticus 11:44 has YHWH self-predicate 'holy' (qadosh) and ground Israel's consecration in it; 1 Peter 1:16 cites that formula directly with the perfect passive (a completed action whose result still stands) 'it stands written' (gegraptai) and 'I am holy' (ego hagios); and Revelation 4:8 echoes the threefold 'holy, holy, holy' (Trisagion) with threefold 'holy' (hagios) of 'Lord God Almighty' (kyrios ho theos ho pantokrator). The only reader divergence is which attested sense of the one root leads, separateness and transcendence or moral purity, and the canon supplies both without ranking them, so neither prong is unsupported.

scripture.reasoning: Direct query of the Hebrew tokens confirms that 'holy' (qadosh, H6918) occurs three consecutive times, then 'YHWH of hosts' (YHWH tsevaoth, meaning the Lord of armies), then the whole earth full of his 'glory' (kavod). Threefold repetition is the strongest superlative construction available in biblical Hebrew, far stronger than the doubled form, and here it elevates the predicate to a unique maximal degree. The 'hosts' (tsevaoth) term binds holiness to majestic transcendence, and the 'glory' (kavod) clause binds it to manifest glory, so both prongs of the proposition stand on one verse.

YHWH (the personal divine name) self-predicates 'holy' (qadosh) with the phrase 'I am YHWH your God, holy am I' (ani YHWH eloheikem, qadosh ani) and uses it as the ground for Israel's consecration through 'consecrate yourselves' (vehitqaddishtem, from the root qadash in the reflexive form, the Hebrew form meaning 'do it to yourself'). So the people's holiness is derived from the divine predicate, not from human achievement. The first-person identity formula ties the moral-purity dimension directly to the divine name. The token order was verified against the Hebrew text.

Direct query shows 'holy' (hagios) applied first to 'the One who called' (ton kalesanta, from kaleo, a completed past action participle in the form that agrees with the caller as direct object) and then 'holy ones' (hagioi) applied to the called community in all their 'conduct' (anastrophe, manner of life). The ethical imperative is grounded in the holiness of the caller, who in context is God. The morphology was confirmed: 'holy' (hagion) sits in apposition (a renaming phrase) to the caller in the direct-object form.

Confirmed by query: the citation formula 'it stands written' (gegraptai, from grapho 'to write', in the perfect passive form, meaning a completed action whose result still stands) introduces the Leviticus statement, 'you shall be holy' (hagioi esesthe), with God speaking in the first person, 'because I am holy' (hoti ego hagios). The perfect passive (a completed action whose result still stands) treats the Torah text (the books of Moses) as standing canonical authority, and the people's commanded holiness is tied back to the divine self-predicate.

Direct query confirms 'holy' (hagios, G0040, in the subject form, masculine singular) three consecutive times, predicated of 'Lord God Almighty' (kyrios ho theos ho pantokrator), then extended by the eternity formula of the one who was and is and is to come. The threefold Greek repetition mirrors the Hebrew 'holy, holy, holy' (Trisagion) of Isaiah 6:3, carrying the Hebrew superlative-by-repetition device into Greek. The acclamation has 'no rest' (anapausin ouk echousin, meaning the worshippers never stop), binding holiness to perpetual worship, divine self-existence (aseity), and 'all-power' (omnipotence).

complicating_texts.resolution: Direct query confirms 'holy' (qadosh, H6918) occurs once in Hosea 11:9, and the surrounding tokens carry the sense that God will not execute the fierceness of his anger because he is God and not man, the 'holy one' (qadosh) in Israel's midst. This complicates any reading of holiness as bare retributive severity, but it confirms the predication of 'holy' (qadosh) to God and shows that holiness can ground mercy that restrains wrath. The verdict (holiness as set-apartness in moral purity and majestic transcendence) is preserved and enriched, not weakened.

Direct query confirms 'holy' (qadosh) occurs twice in Isaiah 57:15. The high and lofty one who inhabits eternity, whose name is 'holy' (qadosh), dwells with the contrite and lowly. This holds transcendence (high and lofty, inhabiting eternity) and moral nearness together in one verse, so the two attested senses of the root are not rivals but complementary. Both prongs of the proposition are supported with no tension.

Query confirms 'holy' (qadosh) predicated of God in Hannah's song (there is none 'holy' (qadosh) like YHWH, the personal divine name). This is a Writings-section witness outside the cult and the prophets, showing the predication is not confined to liturgical or priestly contexts. It strengthens rather than complicates the verdict, included to show the canon spread is genuine and not narrow.

variants.note: The anchor verses are not in the ingested critical-edition window for textual variants (the critical edition covers 3 John 1:1 to 1:15), so no critical apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) was examined; the status 'not_in_ecm_scope' is honestly recorded. The bundle carried zero variant units for these verses. The threefold 'holy' (hagios) in Revelation 4:8 is textually stable across the witnesses queried; the minor known variation in the ordering of the words 'was, is, and is to come' (en, on, and erchomenos) does not touch the predication of holiness, so the verdict is robust against textual variants.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The root q-d-sh (the Hebrew three-letter root behind 'holy') in its strongest sense means set apart, other, separated from the common. On this reading Isaiah 6:3 with 'YHWH of hosts' (the Lord of armies) and the glory ('kavod') filling the earth, and Revelation 4:8 with 'Almighty' (pantokrator) and the eternity formula, foreground God's majestic otherness and transcendence. This lens reads holiness primarily as ontological distance (a distance of being and nature), and it is well grounded in the term and the contexts.

The same root grounds ethical imperatives: Leviticus 11:44 and 1 Peter 1:15-16 derive the people's commanded purity of conduct from God's own holiness, and Isaiah 57:15 ties holiness to dwelling with the contrite. On this reading holiness is primarily moral, the perfection that cannot tolerate sin. This lens is equally well grounded; the vocabulary itself does not rank the two senses, which is why fair readers can foreground either.

Reads Leviticus 11:44 as covenantal holiness predicated on YHWH's own holiness, with 1 Peter 1:15-16 extending the predication into the new-covenant community through the citation formula 'it stands written' (gegraptai). The canonical chain of 'holy' (qadosh) in Hebrew flowing into 'holy' (hagios) in Greek supports this.

Traces 'holy' (qadosh) from the Sinai cult through prophetic theophany (the manifest appearance of God in Isaiah 6) to apocalyptic liturgy (Revelation 4:8), seeing one canonical predicate of God developed across successive contexts and carried from Hebrew into Greek by the same superlative-by-repetition device.

hermeneutics.notes: The proposition is not framework-sensitive at the verdict level: every defensible lens affirms it. The only real divergence is which attested sense of the one root (separateness and transcendence versus moral purity) a reader foregrounds, and the canon supplies both. Both the transcendence lens and the moral-purity lens are stated in their strongest form so neither is strawmanned (misrepresented in a weak form).

stem_audit.notes: The stem describes a lexical predication ('holy', qadosh in Hebrew and hagios in Greek) applied to God across the canon, with two named prongs (moral purity and majestic transcendence) that are both attested senses of the underlying Hebrew root and its Greek counterpart. It does not assume any tradition-specific taxonomy or smuggle a denominational conclusion. The verdict is derived from the queried distribution and morphology (the form-and-grammar pattern), not from the stem's phrasing.

lay_summary: The claim that God is utterly holy, set apart in moral purity and majestic transcendence, rests on a dense word pattern spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical) that the lexical data confirms directly. In Hebrew the adjective 'holy' (qadosh, H6918) is applied to God in 108 places across 94 verses, spread through the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings, with a heavy concentration in Isaiah and the recurring title 'Holy One of Israel'. In Isaiah 6:3 a query of the Hebrew text shows 'holy' (qadosh) repeated three times in a row. That threefold repetition is the strongest intensifier biblical Hebrew has, stronger than simply doubling a word, and here it is joined to 'the Lord of hosts' (YHWH tsevaoth, meaning the Lord of armies) and to the 'glory' (kavod) that fills the earth, which is why the one verse carries both transcendence and majesty. In Leviticus 11:44 God says of himself that he is holy and makes that the reason his people must consecrate themselves, so human holiness is derived from God's, not the other way around. The Greek word 'holy' (hagios, G0040) carries the same idea into the New Testament in 456 places across 241 verses. First Peter 1:16 quotes the Leviticus line word for word with a formula meaning 'it stands written' (gegraptai), and Revelation 4:8 repeats 'holy' (hagios) three times of 'Lord God Almighty' (kyrios ho theos ho pantokrator), mirroring Isaiah in Greek. Where do readers diverge? Only on which of two real senses of the same root leads. The root can mean set apart and other (transcendence) or pure and unable to tolerate sin (moral purity), and the words themselves do not rank these. Texts like Hosea 11:9 and Isaiah 57:15 show God's holiness grounding mercy and nearness to the lowly, not only severity, holding both senses together. Because both senses are attested and neither contradicts the other, the verdict is a high-confidence yes on both prongs.
